messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Captain James "Hawk" Wilson, a seasoned combat pilot with over three decades of service, had always been in control. That was until the day his F-16 malfunctioned during a training exercise, sending him plummeting towards the earth. The explosion that followed still echoed in his mind, a sound that could transport him back to that fateful moment in an instant. The aftermath of the accident left Hawk with more than just physical scars. He began to experience debilitating dizziness and episodes of feeling physically unwell, which would often trigger memories of the crash. The sounds of explosions or bangs would send his heart racing, making him feel like he was reliving the incident all over again. To avoid these triggers, Hawk started to steer clear of hospitals and ambulances, even when his wife, Sarah, fell ill with a minor cold. He couldn't bear the thought of being in a medical setting, surrounded by the sights and smells that reminded him of his own near-death experience. As time passed, Hawk's avoidance behaviors became more entrenched. He stopped enjoying activities he once loved, like flying for recreation or spending time with friends. Instead, he found solace in controlling his eating habits, restricting his diet to feel a sense of control over his body. This coping mechanism made him feel safer, but it also left him feeling numb and disconnected from the world around him. Hawk's body was always on high alert, ready to react to any perceived danger. He would startle at unexpected movements nearby, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. His hypervigilance made it impossible for him to relax, even in the comfort of his own home. Sarah tried to reassure him that he was safe, but Hawk couldn't shake off the feeling that the world was a treacherous place. As the months went by, Hawk's negative appraisals about himself and the world deepened. He felt dead inside, like a part of him had been extinguished in the crash. His once-unshakeable beliefs about the world were shattered, replaced by a pervasive sense of danger lurking around every corner. This new worldview made it even harder for him to confront his triggers or engage in activities that brought him joy. One day, while running errands with Sarah, Hawk was startled by a loud bang from a nearby construction site. The sound sent him reeling, and he quickly ushered Sarah into the car, determined to escape the perceived danger. As they drove away, Hawk realized that his reactions were not just about the trigger itself but also about the feelings of helplessness and fear that it evoked. Hawk's maladaptive strategies had become a self-reinforcing cycle. By avoiding medical cues, he felt safer, but this avoidance also reinforced his negative appraisals about the world. His restricted eating habits made him feel more in control, but they also contributed to his emotional numbness. As Hawk struggled to break free from this cycle, he began to recognize that his behaviors were not only maintaining his PTSD symptoms but also perpetuating his distorted worldview. It was Sarah who finally encouraged Hawk to seek help, worried that his condition would continue to deteriorate if left unaddressed. With a mix of trepidation and hope, Hawk made the decision to confront his demons, aware that the journey ahead would be long and arduous. As he sat in the therapist's office, surrounded by the very medical cues he had been avoiding for so long, Hawk knew that this was just the beginning of his recovery – a journey to reclaim control over his life and find peace in a world that no longer felt safe.
